item.title: Greetings from Senegal, where breakdancers are competing in the Youth Olympics
item.description:
Greetings from Senegal, where breakdancers are competing in the Youth Olympics
November 11, 202612:23 PM ET
By
Ricci Shryock
Ricci Shrylock/NPR
Hip-hop music blasted over a portable speaker while half-a-dozen teenagers practiced their best breakdancing moves in Senagal's capital Dakar. They glided on their shins and jumped into the air, clutched their heels and struck midair poses.
Senegal's breakdancers were honing their craft ahead of the country's historic hosting of the Youth Olympic Games this month. It's the first time an Olympic event is being held on African soil.
I took the photo above last month as 15-year-old Suzanne Toure struck a breakdancing pose. She is the only girl on the Senegal National Sport Dance and Break Team. Three years ago, her little brother introduced her to breakdancing.
Dancers on the Senegalese team mix traditional moves into their routines from national styles such as mbalax and Yela, swirling their arms and legs in a windmill-like motion. "You can sense some American and European influence in our routines, yes, but there are also African dances. It's about mixing these African dances into the breaking," says coach Francis Siméon Gomis.
They see this as their chance to show the world what their nation can offer on the dance floor, and hope to win a medal on home turf.

The gravesite of former President John F. Kennedy at Arlington National Cemetery sits on the same axis as the Lincoln Memorial (seen in the distance). Kennedy's ancestors say Trump's 250-foot arch would not only disrupt the view between the monuments, but cast a shadow over his grave.
Jewel Samad/AFP via Getty Images

One of America's most prominent political dynasties has waded into the growing fight against President Trump's proposed arch in Washington, D.C.
Nine members of the Kennedy family filed suit in federal court on Tuesday to block the 250-foot structure, saying it would obstruct their relatives' gravesites — including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame — at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

item.title: Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
item.description:
Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
Updated November 11, 20265:00 AM ET
Originally published November 11, 20269:19 AM ET
Tamara Keith
Swing voters Theresa from Pennsylvania, Jason from North Carolina and Gerald from Georgia. All three voted in this year's midterms and all three have mixed emotions about the results.
Tara Anand for NPR
hide caption
toggle caption i
Tara Anand for NPR
Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.
"I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."

item.title: Both sides now? Critics slam DOJ moves to dismiss convictions of Trump allies
item.description:
Law
Both sides now? Critics slam DOJ moves to dismiss convictions of Trump allies
November 11, 20265:00 AM ET
Carrie Johnson
Steve Bannon, former adviser to President Trump, attends a pre-trial conference hearing in a fraud case against him in February 2025.
Steven Hirsch/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
toggle caption i
Steven Hirsch/POOL/AFP via Getty Images
The Biden-era Justice Department portrayed the contempt of Congress case against Steve Bannon as open and shut.
Bannon declined to cooperate with the House committee that investigated the siege on the U.S. Capitol, flouting a subpoena and refusing to show up for an interview. A trial jury in Washington, D.C., deliberated for less than three hours before delivering a guilty verdict. A federal appeals court upheld that verdict.
Now, four years later, the DOJ is asking a court to drop the case and erase the conviction "in the interests of justice." Bannon's lawyers do not oppose the move.
Legal experts said it follows a pattern where the Justice Department is helping to wipe the slate clean for allies of President Trump—with no one defending the cases, and without courts hearing arguments to the contrary. item.title: Volunteer musicians play songs for veterans who are hospitalized
item.description:
Volunteer musicians play songs for veterans who are hospitalized
November 11, 20265:00 AM ET
Marisa Peñaloza
After playing and singing "Little Wonders," by Rob Thomas for Army veteran John Fay at the DC VA Medical Center's Hospice Unit, Musicians On Call performer, Dante Ciolfi, thanks Fay for his service.
Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
hide caption
toggle caption i
Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Dante Ciolfi unzips his guitar case in a courtyard of the Veterans Medical Center in Washington, D.C.
"I'm about to tune my guitar," he says.
He is getting ready to play some songs for patients in the hospice wing of the hospital. Ciolfi is a musician volunteer with Musicians On Call or MOC, a non-profit that brings live music to hospital patients nationwide, both bedside and virtually via zoom. The group's motto is "delivering the healing power of music." When Ciolfi isn't volunteering, he teaches computer science to graduate students.
He meets up with Ellen Morris, another volunteer with MOC. She trains musician volunteers on hospital protocols and guides them from room to room.
